title: Sal Amico turns him on to records
summary: Magnarelli could not yet improvise; Amico never explained how but accepted him, gave him exercises and the right records.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: When you went to see them, in your head were you thinking what the heck are those guys thinking about? How did they negotiate their way through these songs? © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -1-

Yeah I thought that, sure. Yeah. I mean I was playing trumpet, not as a professional, but I’d been playing trumpet since I was twelve. And I played piano. You know standing on a bandstand with a rhythm section and improvising on songs, at that level, I had no idea like to learn how to do that. I had no idea.
Right. So if you asked Sal Amico about that, what did he tell you?

Well it’s funny I did sound him out about that. I did ask him. He never really told me. What he did was he accepted me for who I was, he didn’t [inaudible] me the situation. He understood my hunger for the music. And what he did do was he turned me on to the right records. And that was the greatest lesson really I ever had, the first four or five times I went to his house. He did write some things out for me to practice. He heard me play, you know I sat in in the club. So he knew where I was at. He gave me some things to practice and I practiced them. But he never really told me how he does it or how it’s done. And I think he probably thought that, knowing Sal, after I’d known him, of course he passed away, but I’d known him for like fifteen years, I think he probably thought he wasn’t worthy or he couldn’t really do that.
